company.sector: Retail trade via mail order houses or internet

findings.title: Rejecting all cookies leaves 9 of 14 trackers running
findings.why: When someone refuses, the site keeps loading the same third parties it loads for someone who agreed. The refusal is recorded in your banner but never acted on, so nine companies still receive data about that visitor.

evidence.caption: Pass B (reject all) vs Pass C (accept all) — 9 hosts identical

remedy.title: Move the tags behind the consent state
remedy.detail: Your tags fire on page load rather than on the consent event. Wrap each non-essential tag in a consent check and re-publish.

findings.title: You sell a service but publish no data processing agreement
findings.why: Your customers hand you their customers' personal data, which makes you their processor. They are required to have an agreement with you covering it, and right now there is nothing on your site for them to sign or accept.

citations.note: required content of a processor agreement

evidence.caption: /vilkaar and /handelsbetingelser fetched — no Article 28 terms found
lines: searched for: instruction · confidentiality · sub-processor · breach notification · deletion · audit

remedy.title: Generate your processing agreement and sub-processor page
remedy.detail: Drafted from your vendors, where they sit, and what they handle.

findings.title: Contact form posts through an HTTP redirect before reaching TLS
findings.why: The form submits to an address that redirects. For the length of that first request the message and the sender's details travel unencrypted, which anyone on the same network can read.

evidence.caption: Observed on /kontakt
lines: form fields in the first request: navn, email, telefon, besked

remedy.title: Point the form at the https address and add HSTS
remedy.detail: Change the form action to the https address so nothing is sent over the redirect. Then add HSTS, so browsers never try http again.

findings.title: Staff are pasting customer data into a US chat assistant
findings.why: You told us four people use it for customer correspondence. That sends customer names, addresses and order details to a processor you have no agreement with, in a country outside the EEA.

evidence.caption: From your own answer on 4 September
lines: Question: Do staff use AI assistants with customer data?
Answer: Yes — about 4 people, for writing customer replies

remedy.title: Move those four people to GDPR Chat
remedy.detail: Same experience your staff already know, hosted in the EU, with a processing agreement and no training on your content.
remedy.alternativeNote: No free fix exists for this one. Three European alternatives, if you would rather not use ours.

findings.title: Mail and files sit with a US-parented provider
findings.why: Your mail and document storage are with a provider whose ultimate parent is established in the United States. European data residency does not change which courts can compel that parent, and your policy names no basis for the transfer.

evidence.caption: From your DNS records
lines: contracting entity: EU · ultimate parent: US

remedy.title: Compare European alternatives
remedy.detail: Real switching cost, so take your time. Three European-owned options we have checked.
options: Mailbox provider, DE — mail only, keeps your files where they are
Collaboration suite, FR — mail and files, migration tooling included
Collaboration suite, DE — mail and files, on-premise option

findings.title: Session replay records what people type on the checkout page
findings.why: A replay tool is active on the checkout with input masking switched off. It captures keystrokes as they are typed — including the address and card fields — before anyone presses submit.

evidence.caption: Observed on /kassen
lines: www.clarity.ms/tag/... loaded on pass A (before any consent)
fields in scope: navn, adresse, postnr, email, telefon, kortnummer

remedy.title: Turn masking on and exclude the checkout
remedy.detail: Two changes: mask all input by default, and stop the tool loading on the checkout path entirely. The second is the one that matters.

findings.title: Your privacy policy states no retention period for anything
findings.why: People are entitled to know how long you keep their data, for each purpose. Your policy describes what you collect and why, but never says for how long.

evidence.caption: /privatlivspolitik · 2,140 words · searched for a stated duration
lines: searched: opbevar* · slet* · periode · år · måneder · retention
nearest text: "Vi opbevarer dine oplysninger så længe det er nødvendigt."
that phrase is not a period

remedy.title: Rewrite the section from your register
remedy.detail: We need two things from you first — how long you keep orders, and how long you keep newsletter sign-ups. Then the section writes itself from your register.

findings.title: Web fonts load from a US endpoint, sending every visitor's IP address
findings.why: Two fonts are fetched from an external host on every page load. That transmits each visitor's IP address to a third party before they have agreed to anything, and a German court has awarded damages over exactly this.

evidence.caption: Four requests on pass A, before any interaction

remedy.title: Self-host the two fonts
remedy.detail: Download the two families, put them beside your stylesheet, and declare them locally. Nothing leaves your server and the page gets slightly faster.

findings.title: No mention of the right to complain to Datatilsynet
findings.why: Your policy lists most of the rights people have, but omits the right to lodge a complaint with the supervisory authority, which has to be stated.

evidence.caption: /privatlivspolitik · rights section
lines: present: indsigt · berigtigelse · sletning · begrænsning · dataportabilitet

remedy.title: Add the two missing paragraphs
remedy.detail: Two paragraphs, in Danish, naming the right authority for your country and the correct way to withdraw consent for your setup.

findings.title: Newsletter sign-up is bundled with accepting the terms
findings.why: One checkbox at checkout covers both agreeing to the terms and joining the newsletter. Consent to marketing has to be a separate, freely given choice.

evidence.caption: /kassen · single input covering two purposes
lines: label: "Jeg accepterer handelsbetingelserne og vil gerne modtage nyhedsbrevet"
required = true — the order cannot be placed without also joining

remedy.title: Split it into two checkboxes
remedy.detail: Terms stays required. The newsletter becomes a second, optional, unticked box. Your list gets smaller and considerably more valuable.
remedy.snippet:
<label><input type="checkbox" required> Jeg accepterer handelsbetingelserne</label>
<label><input type="checkbox"> Ja tak til nyhedsbrevet</label>

GDPR Art. 28(3).text: Processing by a processor shall be governed by a contract or other legal act under Union or Member State law, that is binding on the processor with regard to the controller and that sets out the subject-matter and duration of the processing, the nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects and the obligations and rights of the controller.

GDPR Art. 30(5).text: The obligations referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to an enterprise or an organisation employing fewer than 250 persons unless the processing it carries out is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, the processing is not occasional, or the processing includes special categories of data as referred to in Article 9(1) or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10.

GDPR Art. 13(2)(a).text: the period for which the personal data will be stored, or if that is not possible, the criteria used to determine that period;

GDPR Art. 83(5).text: Infringements of the following provisions shall, in accordance with paragraph 2, be subject to administrative fines up to 20 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher:

GDPR Art. 44.text: Any transfer of personal data which are undergoing processing or which are intended for processing after transfer to a third country or to an international organisation shall take place only if, subject to the other provisions of this Regulation, the conditions laid down in this Chapter are complied with by the controller and processor, including for onward transfers of personal data from the third country or an international organisation to another third country or to another international organisation.

fine-CNS-02.fragment: What fine could we get for this?
fine-CNS-02.answer: Two different regimes apply, and people usually conflate them. The cookie rule itself comes from the ePrivacy Directive as implemented in Danish law, enforced by Erhvervsstyrelsen, and its penalties are modest. The processing that follows from invalid consent is GDPR, enforced by Datatilsynet, and that is where the large numbers live. For a company your size, Danish practice has been guidance and orders first — fines have followed only when an order was ignored.

grounded.note: We will not invent a number for you. The realistic first outcome is an order with a deadline.

fine-CNS-02.lawNote: The headline maximum. It is a ceiling across the whole Union, not a tariff, and Article 83(2) lists what an authority must weigh before landing anywhere near it.

GDPR Art. 30(5).fragment: The obligations referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to an enterprise or an organisation employing fewer than 250 persons
GDPR Art. 30(5).answer: The exemption reads generously and almost never applies. The three conditions after “unless” are alternatives, so any one of them brings the obligation back — and “the processing is not occasional” catches nearly every business that has customers.
